title: Indian American Cancer Researcher Rachna Shroff Dies at 47 After Terminal Diagnosis
excerpt: University of Arizona oncologist Rachna Shroff, a leading voice on pancreatic and bile duct cancers, died October 11 at 47, weeks after completing a $1.35 million endowment to fund young cancer researchers.
body:
• Dr. Rachna Shroff, an Indian American oncologist and leading expert on pancreatic and bile duct cancers, died on October 11 at age 47, the University of Arizona confirmed on October 12.
  • She was diagnosed in May after a swollen lymph node; testing indicated an aggressive cancer of unknown primary, likely from the stomach or intestine, that had spread and could not be cured.
  • Shroff led the Division of Hematology and Oncology at the University of Arizona College of Medicine – Tucson and was associate director of clinical investigations at its Cancer Center.
  • Before her death she completed a $1.35 million endowment for a Conquer Cancer young investigator award in biliary cancer, which ASCO's foundation says will fund a new researcher every year in perpetuity — readers can support early-career cancer research through that award.

Dr. Rachna Shroff, the Indian American oncologist who became one of the foremost experts on pancreatic and biliary tract cancers, has died at 47. The University of Arizona confirmed the news on October 12, according to USA Today, and The Cancer Letter separately reported that she died on October 11. The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) also mourned her death.

At the University of Arizona, Shroff was associate director of clinical investigations at the Cancer Center and chief of the Division of Hematology/Oncology in the Department of Medicine at the College of Medicine – Tucson. She held an endowed professorship in gastrointestinal oncology.

"I've spent my entire life trying to eradicate cancer."

— Dr. Rachna Shroff, speaking to NBC News before her death

A career built on cancers with few options

Shroff joined the University of Arizona in 2018 after faculty work at MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. The university said she was internationally recognized for work on cholangiocarcinoma, or bile duct cancer, at a time when the rare disease had few treatment options and no FDA-approved therapies. It credited landmark clinical trials she led as principal investigator with helping change that field.

https://x.com/nypost/status/2110659729022214257

According to The Cancer Letter, her focus covered hepatobiliary cancers including cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer and ampulla of Vater cancers — diseases described as understudied and underfunded relative to their mortality. She published more than 80 papers, gave more than 130 presentations, chaired the ASCO Gastrointestinal Cancer Symposium, and served on ASCO's Nominating Committee.

Diagnosis in May, spread within weeks

Shroff sought care for a swollen lymph node in May. Reports based on her interviews with NBC News and Today say testing suggested the cancer had likely originated in her stomach or intestine and had spread by the end of that month. She was told it was terminal adenocarcinoma, a cancer arising in glands lining organs, with no cure available.

Colleagues quoted in coverage described a physician-scientist who kept attending to patients, trials and mentoring even as her own illness advanced, and who joined family milestones in her final months, including her daughter's college visits and her son's baseball games.

Her final project: funding the next researchers

In September, Shroff set out to create a permanent funding source for early-career researchers in her field: the Conquer Cancer–Rachna Shroff, MD, MS, FASCO Young Investigator Award in Biliary Cancer. The university called completing it one of her final wishes.

She reached the goal. About $1.35 million was raised to permanently endow the award — The Cancer Letter says nearly 600 supporters, from colleagues and patients to advocates and industry partners, contributed in about two months. ASCO's Conquer Cancer foundation says the endowment will fund a new researcher every year in perpetuity. For diaspora readers who followed her work, that award is the practical way her mentorship continues: it is specifically aimed at young investigators in biliary cancer, the field she helped build.

Family and legacy

Shroff is survived by her husband, Dr. Puneet Shroff, their two teenage children, Simran and Sachin, her parents and her sister, according to USA Today and other coverage. A Tucson native and daughter of a nephrologist and a biochemist in tributes cited by colleagues, she first worked in a cancer laboratory as a teenager and later trained and taught at some of the country's leading cancer centers.

Her motto, repeated by ASCO in its tribute, was to be the sunshine when you cannot find it. The work she leaves behind is measurable: trials that changed options for bile duct cancer patients, researchers she trained, and an endowed award designed to keep producing both after her death.
